claims.text: At high temperature, plastic strain in fusion plasma-facing structural materials is primarily governed by the stability and distribution of fine grain-boundary precipitates.
At high temperature, toughness in fusion plasma-facing structural materials is primarily governed by the stability and distribution of fine grain-boundary precipitates.
Microalloying can increase the stability and density of fine grain-boundary precipitates.
A titanium addition can promote a more stable and uniform distribution of fine grain-boundary precipitates.
The microalloying-generated precipitates stabilize grain boundaries.
Fine grain-boundary precipitates act as sites for dislocation absorption.
Fine grain-boundary precipitates promote subgrain formation and dynamic recovery.
The modified precipitate population delays grain-boundary sliding at high temperature.
The modified precipitate population delays dislocation pile-up at high temperature.
Delayed grain-boundary sliding and dislocation pile-up increase high-temperature plastic deformation capability.
Relative to the unmodified baseline, the microalloyed material will have greater high-temperature strain to failure.
Relative to the unmodified baseline, the microalloyed material will have improved high-temperature fracture toughness.
The proposed mechanism applies to reduced-activation steels and tungsten alloys under controlled high-temperature tensile deformation when irradiation damage and oxidation do not dominate.
The magnitude of the mechanical improvement depends on microalloy concentration, heat-treatment schedule, and baseline microstructure.
